text.en: Fermentation is one of the oldest and most important biotechnological processes known to humanity. From ancient bread-making to modern bioethanol fuel, the ability of microorganisms to transform simple sugars into valuable products drives an entire global industry. This module explores the **scientific principles**, **conditions**, and **step-by-step production pathway** of ethanol through industrial fermentation.
📚 10 Sections 🎯 10 MCQ Quiz ⏱ ~45 min study 🎓 B.Sc. Level

✓Explain the concept, principle, and types of fermentation.

text.en: Industrial biotechnology applies biological systems — primarily microorganisms and their enzymes — to manufacture products of commercial value at scale.

**Biotechnology** is the application of living organisms, biological systems, or biological processes to develop products and technologies that benefit humanity. When applied at an industrial or manufacturing scale, it is called **Industrial Biotechnology** (also known as _White Biotechnology_).

Unlike medical biotechnology (Red) or agricultural biotechnology (Green), industrial biotechnology focuses on the use of microorganisms, cells, and enzymes to produce chemicals, fuels, food, textiles, and other valuable materials **more sustainably and economically** than conventional chemical processes.

**📌 Industrial Biotechnology — Defined**
Industrial Biotechnology is the **application of biological organisms, systems, or processes in industrial production** to convert raw biological materials (biomass, sugars, starch) into valuable products such as fuels, chemicals, enzymes, food additives, and pharmaceuticals through processes like fermentation.
Use of yeast, bacteria, and fungi to produce ethanol, organic acids, vitamins, and antibiotics.
Isolation and application of enzymes (amylase, lipase, protease) for industrial processes.
Conversion of biomass into bioethanol, biodiesel, and biogas as renewable energy sources.
Design and optimisation of bioreactors, upstream & downstream processing for scale-up production.

**🌿 Advantages Over Conventional Methods**
• Uses renewable raw materials (sugars, starch, biomass) instead of fossil fuels
• Operates under mild conditions (low temperature, ambient pressure) — energy efficient
• Produces fewer toxic by-products — environmentally friendly
• Microorganisms can be genetically improved to enhance yield
• Continuous production possible in bioreactors
• Wide range of products: antibiotics, alcohols, organic acids, vitamins, enzymes
Fermentation is the microbial transformation of organic compounds — typically sugars — into simpler products like alcohol, acids, and gases under controlled conditions.
👆 Click each card to reveal its definition

answer.en: **Fermentation** is a metabolic process in which microorganisms break down organic compounds (sugars) _without the net use of oxygen_ to produce energy, alcohol, acids, or gases. ✓
**Substrate** is the organic material (e.g., glucose, sucrose, starch) that microorganisms use as a raw material and energy source during fermentation. ✓
**Inoculum** is the initial starter culture of microorganisms introduced into the fermentation medium to begin and drive the fermentation process. ✓
**Bioreactor** (fermenter) is a closed vessel designed to provide the optimal environment (temperature, pH, aeration) for large-scale microbial growth and product formation. ✓

text.en: The fundamental principle of fermentation is **anaerobic catabolism of organic compounds**. In the absence of sufficient oxygen, microorganisms cannot carry out full aerobic respiration. Instead, they partially oxidise glucose through _glycolysis_ to produce pyruvate, which is then reduced to various end-products (ethanol, lactic acid, etc.) while regenerating **NAD⁺** to allow glycolysis to continue.
Catalysed by Zymase enzyme complex in _Saccharomyces cerevisiae_

Microorganisms are the **biological catalysts** of fermentation. They possess the specific enzymatic machinery to break down complex substrates into simpler products. Different microorganisms produce different end-products from the same starting material.
_Saccharomyces cerevisiae_ produces **ethanol + CO₂** from glucose. Used in brewing, baking, and bioethanol production.
_Lactobacillus_ sp. converts glucose to **lactic acid**. Used in yoghurt, cheese, silage, and probiotic production.
_Clostridium_ sp. produces **butanol & acetone**; _Acetobacter_ converts ethanol to **acetic acid** (vinegar).
_Aspergillus_ sp. ferments sugars to **citric acid & gluconic acid**. Also produce industrial enzymes like amylase.
Enzymes act as biological catalysts that drive each step of fermentation. Click each accordion panel to explore key enzymes.
**Zymase** is a collective term for the enzyme complex in yeast responsible for alcoholic fermentation. It comprises multiple enzymes working sequentially:

items.en: **Hexokinase** — phosphorylates glucose to glucose-6-phosphate
**Phosphofructokinase** — key regulatory enzyme of glycolysis
**Pyruvate kinase** — produces pyruvate from PEP
**Pyruvate decarboxylase** — converts pyruvate → acetaldehyde + CO₂
**Alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH)** — reduces acetaldehyde → ethanol; regenerates NAD⁺

text.en: **Amylase** hydrolyses starch into fermentable sugars before fermentation begins (saccharification step).

items.en: **α-Amylase** — cleaves internal α-1,4 glycosidic bonds → maltodextrins (liquefaction)
**β-Amylase** — cleaves from non-reducing ends → maltose units
**Glucoamylase** — cleaves glucose units completely for direct fermentation

text.en: Produced by _Aspergillus oryzae_, _Bacillus subtilis_, and added to starch-based fermentation media.
**Invertase** (β-fructofuranosidase) is secreted by _S. cerevisiae_ and hydrolyses sucrose into glucose and fructose — both of which can be directly fermented:

items.en: Sucrose → Glucose + Fructose (both enter glycolysis)
Critical when molasses (sucrose-rich) is used as substrate
Allows yeast to use cane sugar and beet sugar substrates efficiently

text.en: **Lactase** (β-galactosidase) breaks down milk sugar (lactose) into fermentable monosaccharides:

items.en: Used in dairy fermentation (cheese, yoghurt, kefir production)
Also relevant in whey fermentation for bioethanol
Produced by _Lactobacillus_ and _Kluyveromyces marxianus_
Occurs **in the presence of oxygen**
Complete oxidation of substrate to CO₂ & H₂O
High ATP yield (~36–38 ATP per glucose)
Products: CO₂, H₂O, biomass, organic acids
Examples: Citric acid, vinegar, single-cell protein
Used for: antibiotic, enzyme, and vitamin production
Occurs **without oxygen**
Partial oxidation — only 2 ATP per glucose
NAD⁺ regenerated by product formation
Products: ethanol + CO₂, or lactic acid
Examples: Ethanol, lactic acid, biogas
Used for: alcohol, dairy fermentation, silage

text.en:
**📋 Sub-types of Anaerobic Fermentation**
• **Alcoholic fermentation:** Glucose → Ethanol + CO₂ (yeast)
• **Lactic acid fermentation:** Glucose → Lactic acid (bacteria) — homofermentative vs. heterofermentative
• **Butyric acid fermentation:** Glucose → Butyric acid + H₂ + CO₂ (_Clostridium_)
• **Propionic acid fermentation:** Lactic acid → Propionic acid + CO₂ (_Propionibacterium_)
Efficient fermentation requires careful optimisation of substrate, microbial strain, and physicochemical parameters. Any deviation from optimal conditions reduces yield significantly.
Carbon and energy source for the microorganism. Must be soluble and at optimum concentration (10–20% for ethanol).
Must be pure culture, high-yielding strain, alcohol-tolerant, and capable of growing rapidly on available substrate.
Optimal for yeast: 28–32°C. High temperature denatures enzymes; low temperature slows metabolism and growth.
Slightly acidic pH optimal for yeast. Low pH prevents bacterial contamination. pH <4 or >6 inhibits fermentation.
Minimal O₂ for alcoholic fermentation. Small amounts needed for yeast growth initially; then sealed for anaerobic production.
Nitrogen source (ammonium sulfate), phosphate, potassium, magnesium, and vitamins like biotin and thiamine are essential.
The substrate must be **rich in fermentable sugars** and cost-effective. Key substrates include:

items.en: **Molasses** — by-product of sugar refining; contains 50–55% sucrose; cheap & widely used
**Sugarcane juice** — direct source of sucrose; used in Brazil and India
**Corn/wheat starch** — requires saccharification (amylase treatment) before fermentation
**Cellulosic biomass** — requires pre-treatment + cellulase; used for second-generation ethanol

text.en: Optimal sugar concentration: **10–20% w/v**. Above 20%, osmotic stress inhibits yeast; below 5%, low product yield.
Temperature directly affects enzyme activity and cell growth:

items.en: Optimal range for _S. cerevisiae_: **28–32°C**
Below 20°C: Greatly reduced metabolic rate — slow fermentation
Above 40°C: Enzymes denatured; cell death; fermentation stops
Industrial fermenters use **cooling jackets** to control exothermic heat released
Thermotolerant strains (optimum ~38–40°C) reduce cooling costs in tropical countries

text.en: pH impacts enzyme activity and microbial competition:

items.en: Optimal pH for yeast fermentation: **4.5–5.5**
pH 4.5 minimises contamination by acid-sensitive bacteria
pH above 6 favours bacterial contaminants (lactic acid bacteria)
pH is maintained using phosphate buffers or by controlled addition of H₂SO₄ / NaOH
As fermentation proceeds, CO₂ production naturally lowers pH (carbonic acid)

text.en: 🌀 Oxygen Availability — Aerobic vs Anaerobic Phases ▼
Oxygen requirement differs by fermentation phase:

items.en: **Phase 1 (Aerobic — Growth):** Limited aeration allows yeast biomass multiplication
**Phase 2 (Anaerobic — Production):** Vessel sealed; anaerobic conditions shift yeast metabolism to ethanol production (Pasteur Effect)
High O₂ → _Crabtree effect_: yeast produces ethanol even in aerobic conditions at high glucose
Industrial practice: Sparging with N₂ gas to create fully anaerobic conditions in sealed bioreactors

text.en: Beyond carbon (substrate), yeast requires macro- and micro-nutrients:

items.en: **Nitrogen:** Ammonium sulfate [(NH₄)₂SO₄] or urea — for amino acid and protein synthesis
**Phosphorus:** Monopotassium phosphate (KH₂PO₄) — for ATP, nucleic acids
**Magnesium:** MgSO₄ — enzyme cofactor (hexokinase, enolase)
**Vitamins:** Biotin, thiamine (B₁), pantothenic acid — for enzyme function
**Molasses supplementation:** Usually provides sufficient trace elements naturally

text.en:
**⚠️ Inhibitors of Fermentation**
• **Ethanol toxicity:** >14–15% v/v ethanol inhibits yeast growth (product inhibition)
• **Osmotic stress:** Very high sugar concentration dehydrates cells
• **Contamination:** Competing bacteria produce acids that lower yield
• **Heavy metals:** Copper, zinc at high concentrations inhibit enzymes
• **Temperature extremes:** >40°C denatures critical fermentation enzymes
Fermentation is the backbone of numerous industries, providing sustainable routes to produce medicines, fuels, food products, and industrial chemicals.

text.en:
**🌍 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) & Fermentation**
• **SDG 7 (Clean Energy):** Bioethanol as renewable transport fuel reduces fossil fuel dependency
• **SDG 3 (Good Health):** Fermentation-derived antibiotics and vaccines save millions of lives annually
• **SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption):** Agro-industrial waste (molasses, bagasse) converted to valuable products
• **SDG 13 (Climate Action):** Bioethanol reduces net CO₂ emissions vs. petrol; CO₂ released was first fixed by plants
• **India context:** India is the 3rd largest ethanol producer globally; National Biofuel Policy targets 20% ethanol blending by 2025
Ethanol (C₂H₅OH) is produced industrially through the anaerobic fermentation of sugar-rich substrates by _Saccharomyces cerevisiae_. It is the world's most produced biofuel.
By-product of sugar cane/beet processing. Contains **45–55% fermentable sugars** (mainly sucrose). Cheapest and most widely used substrate in India and Brazil.
Fresh expressed juice with **12–18% sucrose**. Direct and efficient substrate; Brazil's primary ethanol source (~30 billion litres/year).
Corn, wheat, cassava, potato. Requires **saccharification** (enzymatic hydrolysis of starch by amylase) to glucose before fermentation. Primary substrate in USA (corn).
Agricultural waste: sugarcane bagasse, rice straw, corn stover. Requires **pre-treatment + cellulase**. Not yet commercially dominant but growing rapidly.

**🦠 Why _Saccharomyces cerevisiae_ (Baker's/Brewer's Yeast)?**
• **High ethanol yield:** Converts ~90–95% of theoretical maximum glucose to ethanol
• **Ethanol tolerance:** Survives up to 14–15% v/v ethanol (flocculent strains up to 20%)
• **GRAS status:** Generally Recognised As Safe — used in food and drink
• **Fast growth:** Doubling time ~90 minutes under optimal conditions
• **Facultative anaerobe:** Can grow both aerobically (biomass) and anaerobically (ethanol)
• **Well-characterised:** Fully sequenced genome; amenable to genetic improvement
Alcoholic fermentation proceeds in **two main stages**: glycolysis (in the cytoplasm) followed by pyruvate reduction to ethanol.
C₆H₁₂O₆ + 2 ADP + 2 Pᵢ + 2 NAD⁺ → 2 CH₃COCOOH (Pyruvate) + 2 ATP + 2 NADH + 2 H₂O
CH₃CHO + NADH + H⁺ —[Alcohol dehydrogenase]→ C₂H₅OH (Ethanol) + NAD⁺
NAD⁺ regenerated here allows glycolysis to continue continuously
Theoretical yield: 51.1 g ethanol per 100 g glucose (Gay-Lussac's equation)
Click on each step in the **Interactive Flowchart** (next chapter) to explore details. Here is a concise overview:

rows.en: Conversion of sugars to ethanol + CO₂
Measure Brix, pH, ethanol, cell density

text.en: Blended with petrol as **E5, E10, E20**; reduces GHG emissions. India targets E20 blend by 2025 under National Biofuel Policy.
70% ethanol is a potent antiseptic. Widely used in hand sanitisers, pharmaceutical cleaning, and hospital disinfection.
Solvent for resins, dyes, perfumes, pharmaceuticals, and cosmetics. Used in extraction, printing, and textile industries.
Base of beer (~4–5%), wine (~12%), whisky (~40%), and other alcoholic drinks produced by yeast fermentation.
Precursor for acetic acid, ethyl acetate, diethyl ether, acetaldehyde, and polyethylene (bio-based plastic).
Solvent and preservative in medicines, cough syrups, tinctures, and extraction of plant-based active compounds.

items.en: 1 **Raw Material Preparation** Collection and processing of substrate 🌾 **Raw Material Preparation:** • **Molasses:** Diluted with water to 10–18° Brix (sugar content); adjusted to pH 4.5–5.0 • **Sugarcane:** Juice expressed by crushing; clarified by settling or centrifugation • **Starch sources:** Milled to flour → cooked at 120–150°C → treated with _α-amylase_ (liquefaction) then _glucoamylase_ (saccharification) to release glucose • Mineral nutrients (N, P, Mg) and vitamins added to the medium ▼

2 **Medium Sterilisation** Elimination of contaminating microorganisms 🔥 **Medium Sterilisation:** • Heating medium to **80–100°C** for 10–30 minutes kills most bacteria and wild yeast • For molasses: often acidification to pH 3.5–4.0 is sufficient to reduce contamination risk • Industrial fermenters use **continuous sterilisation** (flash heat exchange) — faster and energy-efficient • Cooling to inoculation temperature (28–32°C) before yeast addition is essential ▼

3 **Inoculation** Addition of yeast starter culture 🦠 **Inoculation:** • _Saccharomyces cerevisiae_ starter culture prepared in a **seed fermenter** (smaller vessel) • Yeast pre-grown aerobically to build up high cell density (**10⁷–10⁸ cells/mL**) • Inoculation rate: **2–5% v/v** of the main fermenter volume • Active Dry Yeast (ADY) or Compressed Yeast may also be used for industrial batches • Inoculum viability must be ≥90% (checked by methylene blue or trypan blue exclusion) ▼

4 **Fermentation** Anaerobic sugar-to-ethanol conversion 🏺 **Fermentation Phase:** • Bioreactor sealed; anaerobic conditions maintained (**N₂ sparging or CO₂ blanket**) • Temperature: **28–32°C** (controlled by cooling jacket — reaction is exothermic) • pH: maintained at **4.5–5.5** • Duration: **24–72 hours** depending on substrate and strain • Yeast converts glucose → ethanol + CO₂ via Embden–Meyerhof–Parnas pathway • CO₂ produced (≈ 44 g per 100 g glucose) must be vented safely • Final ethanol concentration in _fermented wash_: typically **8–12% v/v** ▼

5 **Ethanol Formation Monitoring** Process analytics and end-point detection 📊 **Monitoring Parameters:** • **Brix (°Bx):** Measures residual sugar concentration — fermentation complete when Brix drops to <2° • **Ethanol content:** Measured by ebulliometer, GC, or specific gravity • **pH:** Monitored continuously; controlled by buffer additions • **Cell count:** Yeast viability and density by microscopy or coulter counter • **CO₂ evolution:** Rate of gas production indicates fermentation activity • Online sensors (pH electrode, dissolved O₂ probe) used in modern plants ▼

6 **Distillation** Separation of ethanol from fermented wash 🏗️ **Distillation:** • Fermented wash (8–12% ethanol) pumped to **distillation columns** • Ethanol boils at **78.4°C**; water boils at 100°C — difference allows separation • **Analyser column:** Strips ethanol from the wash; produces vapour of ~40–50% ethanol • **Rectifier column:** Concentrates ethanol to **95–96%** (azeotropic limit) • Bottom product (slop/stillage) contains water, yeast, and organic residues — used as animal feed or fertiliser • Energy integration: heat recovery systems reduce steam consumption ▼

7 **Dehydration & Purification** Producing anhydrous (fuel-grade) ethanol 💎 **Dehydration to Anhydrous Ethanol:** • 95–96% ethanol forms a **water-ethanol azeotrope** — cannot be further concentrated by simple distillation • Methods to break azeotrope: – **Molecular sieves (zeolite 3Å):** Adsorb water selectively — most common modern method – **Azeotropic distillation:** Add benzene or cyclohexane as entrainer – **Vacuum distillation** or **pervaporation membranes** • Final product: **Anhydrous ethanol ≥99.5%** suitable for fuel blending (E5–E20) • Fuel ethanol is **denatured** with 2–5% petrol to prevent consumption

text.en:
**📌 Key Process Parameters Summary**
• Substrate concentration: **10–18° Brix**
• Fermentation temperature: **28–32°C**
• pH: **4.5–5.5**
• Fermentation time: **24–72 hours**
• Ethanol in wash: **8–12% v/v**
• Final ethanol purity: **95–99.5%**
Consolidated revision points for exam preparation. Review these before your examination.
**Industrial Biotechnology** (White Biotechnology) applies microorganisms/enzymes for large-scale manufacture of chemicals, fuels, food, and pharmaceuticals.
**Fermentation** is the microbial anaerobic breakdown of organic compounds (sugars) to produce energy, alcohol, acids, or gases.
The **principle** is NAD⁺ regeneration: NADH produced in glycolysis is re-oxidised by reducing pyruvate to ethanol or lactate, allowing continuous glycolysis.
**Key enzyme for alcoholic fermentation:** Pyruvate decarboxylase (pyruvate → acetaldehyde) and Alcohol dehydrogenase (acetaldehyde → ethanol + NAD⁺).
**Net equation:** C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2 C₂H₅OH + 2 CO₂ + 2 ATP (Gay-Lussac; yield = 51.1 g ethanol per 100 g glucose).
**Optimal conditions for yeast fermentation:** Temperature 28–32°C; pH 4.5–5.5; sugar concentration 10–18°Brix; anaerobic; nutrients (N, P, Mg).
**_Saccharomyces cerevisiae_** is the preferred organism for ethanol production — facultative anaerobe, ethanol-tolerant (up to 14–15%), GRAS, high yield, well-characterised genome.
**Raw materials:** Molasses (cheapest; 50–55% sucrose), Sugarcane juice (direct), Starch sources (corn, wheat — require saccharification by amylase).
**Ethanol production steps:** Raw material prep → Sterilisation → Inoculation → Fermentation (28–32°C, 24–72 h) → Distillation (78.4°C) → Rectification (95–96%) → Dehydration (≥99.5%).
**95–96% ethanol = azeotropic** (cannot be purified further by simple distillation). Molecular sieves or azeotropic distillation needed for anhydrous (fuel-grade) ethanol.
**Aerobic fermentation** (O₂ present): high ATP yield, products = CO₂ + H₂O + biomass; used for antibiotics, citric acid, enzymes. **Anaerobic**: 2 ATP, products = ethanol or lactic acid.
**Product inhibition:** Ethanol >14–15% v/v inhibits yeast. This limits single-batch ethanol concentration, requiring distillation for concentration.
**Applications of ethanol:** Biofuel (E10, E20 blending), antiseptic (70%), solvent, chemical feedstock (acetaldehyde, ethyl acetate), beverages, pharmaceutical solvent.
**India's Ethanol Programme:** National Biofuel Policy (2018) targets 20% ethanol blending in petrol (E20) by 2025–26, primarily using molasses and damaged food grains.
Important scientific terms with simple, student-friendly definitions for quick revision and exam preparation.

definition.en: The microbial metabolic process of **partial anaerobic breakdown of organic compounds** (sugars) to produce energy, alcohol, organic acids, or gases without the net consumption of oxygen.
The **starting material or carbon source** (e.g., glucose, sucrose, starch, molasses) that microorganisms use as food and energy source during fermentation.
A **small quantity of active starter culture** of the desired microorganism added to a fermentation medium to initiate the fermentation process.
A **controlled vessel or tank** designed to provide optimal physical and chemical conditions (temperature, pH, aeration) for large-scale microbial growth and product synthesis.
The most widely used **yeast in industrial fermentation**. Also called baker's yeast or brewer's yeast; converts sugars to ethanol + CO₂ under anaerobic conditions. GRAS status.
The **first stage of sugar metabolism** occurring in the cytoplasm, converting one glucose (6C) into two pyruvate molecules (3C) with a net gain of 2 ATP and 2 NADH.
The **enzyme complex in yeast** responsible for alcoholic fermentation. Includes key enzymes like pyruvate decarboxylase and alcohol dehydrogenase. Discovered by Eduard Buchner (1897).
The enzyme that catalyses the **final step of alcoholic fermentation**: reducing acetaldehyde to ethanol using NADH, thereby regenerating NAD⁺ for continued glycolysis.
A **thick dark syrup by-product** of sugar refining containing 45–55% fermentable sugars. The cheapest and most commonly used substrate for industrial ethanol fermentation.
The enzymatic **hydrolysis of starch or cellulose into fermentable sugars** (glucose, maltose) using amylase or cellulase enzymes as a preparatory step before fermentation.
A **separation technique** using differences in boiling points to separate ethanol (bp 78.4°C) from water (bp 100°C) in the fermented wash to concentrate the product.

A **constant-boiling mixture** of ethanol and water (95.6% ethanol: 4.4% water) that cannot be separated further by simple distillation. Dehydration requires molecular sieves or azeotropic distillation.
The **inhibition of fermentation by oxygen**, observed by Louis Pasteur. In aerobic conditions, yeast uses aerobic respiration; in anaerobic conditions, it switches to fermentation for energy.
Ethanol produced by **biological fermentation of biomass** (sugarcane, corn, cellulose) used as a renewable fuel. Blended with petrol (E5–E20) to reduce fossil fuel dependence and GHG emissions.

Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide — a crucial **electron carrier coenzyme**. NAD⁺ (oxidised) accepts electrons in glycolysis to form NADH. In fermentation, NADH is re-oxidised back to NAD⁺, allowing glycolysis to continue.

**Ethanol with ≥99.5% purity** (virtually water-free), produced by molecular sieve dehydration. Required for fuel-grade ethanol to prevent engine corrosion and phase separation when blended with petrol.
